rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to identify which critical pairs respond to slope, especially the late co-elution. This diagnostic run will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature tuning.

The late co-elution barely responds to gradient slope, so test a substantial temperature shift for selectivity. Retain the first gradient to isolate temperature effects and keep the last peak below ten minutes.

Lower temperature should improve the early critical pair, while a higher starting organic fraction permits a shallower gradient without extending the late elution time. This also tests whether shifting the gradient window helps the persistent late cluster.

Shift to a narrower, shallower gradient to improve the middle critical pairs while offsetting the added gradient duration with a higher starting organic fraction. Monitor early-peak compression and whether the late co-elution separates.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the remaining middle and late critical pairs while keeping the early separation close to the best run. The last peak should remain near the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Test a lower starting fraction with a slightly steeper slope to strengthen the middle critical separation without materially extending the run. This distinguishes starting-composition effects from slope effects near the current optimum.
Test a shallower gradient with a higher start to improve the late cluster while keeping the last peak near ten minutes. The main tradeoff to monitor is compression of the earlier peaks.

Test temperature at the best narrowed gradient to check for selectivity changes that were not apparent in the broad scout. Earlier elution may also create room for a slightly shallower gradient afterward.

Keep the initial slope of injection 7 but end the gradient before the late cluster elutes, testing whether a terminal hold improves its persistent co-elution. The moderately strong final solvent limits the risk of excessive retention.

Explore a substantially higher starting fraction and shallower slope to test a different selectivity regime, particularly for the late cluster. This is an exploratory tradeoff: late separation may improve, but early peaks may compress or change order.

Move the terminal hold earlier so it affects the late cluster rather than only the last two peaks. The faster initial gradient should offset some hold-related delay and test whether constant-solvent selectivity can break the persistent co-elution.

Test a distinctly steeper gradient at low temperature to look for a favorable selectivity regime across the observed middle-pair crossings. The low starting fraction protects early retention, and the short gradient leaves ample margin below the time penalty.

Return to low-temperature refinement near the best methods, using an intermediate starting fraction and slope. This should preserve early resolution while testing the balance between the middle critical pair and late-cluster separation below ten minutes.

Test a small temperature increase from injection 6 to remove its slight time penalty while retaining most of its favorable selectivity. This checks whether the local optimum lies between the tested 25 and 40 C conditions.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 5 and 6, targeting improved critical-pair resolution without crossing the ten-minute penalty threshold. The final composition should remain above the last peak’s elution composition.
Check a single temperature step above the best method to confirm whether its middle-pair selectivity can improve. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates this small temperature effect.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 15 to improve the middle critical pair and late cluster. The modest temperature increase should keep the last peak close to ten minutes despite the shallower gradient.

Test a slope between injections 6 and 16, with the terminal hold beginning after the critical late cluster. This may retain most of injection 6’s resolution while keeping the last peak near ten minutes.

Bracket the best method with a slightly shallower gradient to measure whether improved critical-pair resolution outweighs the expected small time penalty. This directly tests the remaining slower-side boundary around injection 7.

Refine the higher-starting-fraction branch with a slightly shallower slope than injection 8. This tests whether gains in the middle and late critical pairs can outweigh early-pair compression while keeping the last peak near ten minutes.

Test the shallower side of injection 14 to strengthen its two middle critical pairs. This checks whether their resolution gains can outweigh the modest expected time penalty at a lower starting fraction.

Combine a shallower gradient with intermediate temperature to target better middle-pair separation while keeping the last peak near ten minutes. This tests a remaining local tradeoff between temperature-driven early compression and slope-driven resolution gains.

Test the slightly shallower neighbor of injection 6 at the temperature that has consistently given the best selectivity. This directly checks whether improved middle and late resolution compensates for the expected small time penalty.

Use the final injection to test a shallower neighbor of injection 4, targeting improved middle-pair resolution with the last peak close to ten minutes. Keep 25 C, which has consistently provided the strongest overall selectivity.
